reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in FBN1, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1; roughly a quarter of cases arise from de novo variants
Diagnosis rests on the revised Ghent criteria, which weight aortic root dilatation and ectopia lentis as cardinal features alongside a systemic score and family history
Skeletal features include disproportionately long limbs and digits (arachnodactyly), tall stature, pectus deformity, scoliosis, joint hypermobility, and a high-arched palate
Ectopia lentis (typically superotemporal lens dislocation) is a hallmark ocular finding and helps distinguish Marfan syndrome from Loeys-Dietz syndrome
Progressive aortic root dilatation at the sinuses of Valsalva predisposes to aortic dissection and is the principal cause of premature death
Lifelong surveillance with transthoracic echocardiography, blood-pressure control, and medical aortic protection (beta-blockers and/or angiotensin-receptor blockers) are central to management
Prophylactic aortic root surgery is considered once the aortic diameter reaches an at-risk threshold or shows rapid progression, individualised to body size and family history
Activity advice usually restricts high-intensity isometric exercise, competitive contact sport, and heavy lifting to reduce aortic wall stress
reference.pathophysiology: Marfan syndrome results from loss of normal fibrillin-1, a glycoprotein that assembles into microfibrils forming the scaffold of elastic fibres in the aorta, suspensory ligament of the lens, skin, and periosteum. Deficient or abnormal microfibrils weaken these connective tissues and also dysregulate transforming growth factor beta signalling, since microfibrils normally sequester latent TGF-beta. Excess TGF-beta activity contributes to progressive weakening and dilatation of the aortic media, degeneration of the zonular fibres causing lens subluxation, and overgrowth of the long bones. The combined structural and signalling defects explain the cardiovascular, ocular, skeletal, and dural manifestations.
additionalDifferentials: Homocystinuria (which can also cause ectopia lentis and a marfanoid habitus)
MASS phenotype and isolated familial thoracic aortic aneurysm
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography with aortic root measurement indexed to body size
Slit-lamp examination through a dilated pupil to detect ectopia lentis
Cross-sectional aortic imaging (CT or MR angiography) to assess the whole aorta
Molecular genetic testing of FBN1 and, where indicated, a wider aortopathy gene panel
Plasma homocysteine or urine amino acids to exclude homocystinuria
Imaging for dural ectasia and skeletal review for scoliosis and protrusio acetabuli
redFlags: Sudden severe chest, back, or abdominal pain suggesting acute aortic dissection
Rapidly enlarging aortic root or diameter approaching the surgical threshold
New aortic regurgitation or signs of cardiac failure
Sudden painless visual loss suggesting retinal detachment or acute lens dislocation
Symptoms of pneumothorax such as acute breathlessness and pleuritic pain
reference.prognosis: With regular cardiovascular surveillance, medical aortic protection, and timely prophylactic surgery, life expectancy now approaches that of the general population. Untreated aortic disease carries a high risk of dissection and premature death, so adherence to monitoring and lifestyle advice is critical.
pitfalls: Attributing tall marfanoid habitus to Marfan syndrome without excluding homocystinuria, which needs different management
Relying on a single aortic measurement rather than tracking the trend over time
Overlooking non-aortic vascular and ocular complications during follow-up
Failing to offer cascade family screening and genetic counselling
Assuming a normal childhood echocardiogram excludes future aortic disease
references: Revised Ghent nosology for the Marfan syndrome
management: Provide medical aortic protection with beta-blockers and/or angiotensin-receptor blockers to slow aortic root dilatation
Maintain lifelong cardiovascular surveillance with serial transthoracic echocardiography, blood-pressure control and periodic whole-aorta cross-sectional imaging
Advise activity modification, avoiding isometric exertion and high-intensity contact or competitive sport
Undertake prophylactic aortic root surgery when the root reaches the surgical threshold or shows rapid growth or a family history of dissection
Manage acute aortic dissection as an emergency with heart-rate and blood-pressure control and immediate surgery for type A dissection
Provide ophthalmic care for ectopia lentis with refractive correction and amblyopia management
Monitor and manage skeletal features including scoliosis and pectus deformity and treat symptomatic dural ectasia
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant FBN1 disease with cascade family screening and pre-pregnancy counselling with close monitoring in pregnancy
